en: The *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sundarika*, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi in the Wu Kingdom.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, dwelling in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In the grove, there were a great many *bhikṣus*, and the Buddha preached the Sūtra for them.
At that time, there was a Brahmin named Sundarika who, upon seeing the Buddha from afar, stopped and stood leaning on his staff with his tongue protruding, thinking to himself:
"I bathe three times a day, eat fruit, and drink water; I do not accept the offerings of others."
"I practice the superior conduct of a śramaṇa.
You people delight in fine food, fine clothing, and warm bedding; you feign being sages while being untrue, and thus do not equal my Way.
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the brahmin's mind, addressed the śramaṇas, saying:
“Furthermore, there are twenty-one evils in the conduct of a woman that prevent her from obtaining fine food and elegant clothing:
her mind is set on lewdness;
her mind is set on anger; [and so forth].”
Their intent is set on folly;
their intent is set on sleep;
their intent is set on stagnation, which is to say, they lack proper deportment.
Their intent is set on arrogance;
their intent is set on conceit;
their intent is set on envy.
Their intent is set on stinginess and greed;
their intent is set on cruelty and violence, lacking any heart of compassion;
their intent is set on hypocrisy, with inner and outer being at odds.
Their will is set on shamelessness, lacking a sense of inner remorse;
their will is set on foul conduct, feeling no personal shame or abhorrence;
their will is set on those evils, yet they do not perceive them for themselves.
Their will is set on licentiousness, yet their words do not praise integrity;
their will is set on social chatter, yet they foster the two evils of slander;
their will is set on conflict, yet they do not resolve the two disputes.
If one's will is set on impoliteness, one will naturally fail to be humble;
if one's will is set on persisting in error, one will not accept the admonitions of the virtuous;
if one's will is set on filial impiety, one will extinguish compassion and delight in contrariness.

Their aspirations are set upon heterodox paths, and they venerate malevolent spirits and charms; their family wealth is exhausted until their kin fall into poverty, yet they remain unaware of this extraordinary calamity. Failing to take refuge in the Triple Gem, they indulge in fine food and elegant clothing, following their desires in luxury.
Because these twenty-one evils defile and disorder the mind, it is like attempting to cleanse filth by staining it with colors; there is not one benefit in ten thousand.
To harbor such manifold evils is to enter the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm after death, where the suffering is immeasurable.

"The śramaṇa beholds the Buddha’s luminous precepts; he discards the old and renews himself, refining his emotions and extinguishing desire. Being pure within and without, he is like a clean cloth that takes on color when dyed, becoming an object of contemplation for the multitude."

When a śramaṇa perceives the light, his conduct is lofty and his wisdom is sufficient; though the world offers him clothing, food, and dwellings, he accepts them without fault, and the merit of the donor is great.
He practices meditative concentration and attains the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat; this is heard by people as well.

Although the śramaṇa has not yet attained the Way, he clarifies the meaning of the Buddha’s scriptures, maintains a rectified mind, and is filial toward the teachings. He spreads universal compassion and nurtures all beings, extending his grace to the multitude of living things. By taking himself as a measure to bring peace to others, he regards enemies as his own children. When he sees a woman approaching, he treats her as a sister;

if he beholds those in poverty and suffering, he should contemplate the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, vowing that all beings may have peace of body and joy of mind, encounter the Triple Gem, have their defilements removed and darkness extinguished, attain purity of mind and clarity of vision, return to original non-being, and enjoy eternal, boundless peace.
With such conduct and resolve, one remains forever free from fault regarding fine food and elegant clothing.
Yet the fundamental nature of all living beings is characterized by greed, lust, anger, hatred, ignorance, and jealousy; they are the dregs among the turbid and the darkness within the dark.

The śramaṇa’s mind opened and he received illumination; the defilement of ignorance was entirely stilled. Although he dwells in this impure world, he is like a lotus flower situated within the mud: the mud cannot stain the flower, and thus receiving alms incurs no fault.

If one harbors the three poisons and does not eliminate the ten evils, indulging the mind in lustful desires and seeking gratification through flattery and deception, failing to uphold the Buddha's precepts—it would be better to swallow glowing iron and drink molten copper.
"Such a person dies in an instant, having received offerings with defiled intent; upon death, they enter Mount Tai, where they drink molten copper and eat charcoal for years beyond calculation.
The Brahmin stepped forward and said to the Buddha, "I wish to go and bathe.
There is a stream named Hao-shou; whoever enters it to bathe shall have the impurities of their mind washed away by the flowing water."
"Ever since hearing my father’s instruction, I have bathed three times every day.
The Buddha said to the brahmin, "This land has many streams; by bathing in them, can people attain liberation from suffering?"
"One who bathes a thousand times may remove the impurities of the body, but what can they do for the impurities of the mind?
My śramaṇas have severed all seeking and contemplate emptiness; they do not desire the three realms, and as the impurities of their minds are extinguished, they attain the path of purity."
"From which teacher have you received the bath of the water of the Dharma?
Have you thereby removed the defilements of the mind? He replied:
"My father said this. The Buddha asked,
"Has your father attained the Way?"
He replied, "No. The Buddha said:
"My Way issues from the mind; when the mind is upright and the will is pure, one attains the Way.
The Brahmin knelt on his right knee and said:
"Just now, as I leaned on my staff and stuck out my tongue, I was merely acting out of madness and folly."
Now that I have heard the Buddha’s sutras, my mind has finally awakened; it is as if a lamp has appeared in the darkness, and for the first time I possess eyes.
I beg to become a śramaṇa; I pray that the Buddha will compassionately accept me!
The Buddha said, "If there are relatives, repay them. He replied:
"He has no kinsmen.
The Buddha said, "Śramaṇa, come."

Having thus become a śramaṇa, he sat beneath a tree and contemplated twenty-one matters; casting off all sensual desires, his mind suddenly became free of discursive thought, and he immediately attained the path of Arhatship.
He went to where the Buddha was and, placing his head at the Buddha’s feet, said:
“Now the blind have regained their sight, and the mad have been cured.
The Buddha said:
"Is this path excellent?
Or is the path you follow excellent? He replied:
"All other paths are deviant; only the Buddha's path is correct.
The Buddha told the śramaṇas:
"If you thoroughly contemplate twenty-one matters, the Way can be attained."
Upon hearing this sutra, the śramaṇas rejoiced, paid their respects, and withdrew.
Thus ends the *Sūtra on Sundarika*.
